source.title: Scalable Data Synthesis through Human-like Cognitive Imitation and Data Recombination
source.authors: Zhongyi Ye; Weitai Zhang; Xinyuan Zhou; Yongxin Zhu; N. Rao; En-Hong Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study varies synthetic-data training scale and measures downstream benchmark accuracy, which tests V6 conceptually. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit the parameter, token, or compute scaling laws in V1–V3.
record.gate_note: The cited scaling laws appear as background motivation only. The study reports downstream math-task accuracy after continued pretraining on synthetic data, including accuracy-versus-training-token plots. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits or extrapolations, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: This is a data-synthesis method paper. It cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as motivation. Its results are downstream math accuracy after continued pretraining on its own synthetic data (CCS), compared with base models and other synthetic datasets, plus accuracy-versus-token curves for its own data variants. It reports no held-out loss, no power-law fit or extrapolation, and no compute allocation. It makes no claim that downstream accuracy is predictable from scale or loss. The 'scalability' it studies is how useful its synthetic data stays as volume grows. That is a property of its own method, not a test of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that CCS's knowledge-to-skill mapping gives higher learning efficiency than other synthesis methods. They say CCS synthetic data scales beyond 100B tokens, with diversity, accuracy and complexity as the key factors, and that it reaches Qwen2.5-Math-level performance. They make no claim about scaling laws in the Kaplan/Hoffmann sense.
record.recipe_differences: Continued pretraining on synthetic mathematical data with downstream accuracy evaluation; no held-out cross-entropy measurement, power-law fit, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream accuracy varies with seed diversity, explanation-style diversity, filtering and answer accuracy, question difficulty, and model size; the 72B model is reported to plateau or degrade on unfiltered data.

fits_no_version.finding: In continued pretraining of Qwen2.5-1.5B, downstream math accuracy keeps rising up to 30B synthetic tokens for filtered or competition-level data. It plateaus for unfiltered QME (around 25B) and for K12-level data. The 72B model plateaus or degrades on unfiltered data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains in downstream accuracy from scaling synthetic continued-pretraining data depend on data accuracy, diversity and difficulty, and saturate for low-quality or easy data.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (2025)
record.problems: No held-out loss or scaling-law fits are reported. The accuracy-versus-token results are plotted without numerical values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The reported accuracy trends depend on synthetic-data quality and difficulty.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no parameter, token or compute sweep.
No fits on small runs and no predictions of larger runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law form is fitted in any regime, including synthetic-data continued pretraining.
There is no fit or prediction of downstream accuracy from scale or loss. Accuracy-versus-token curves are only figure-level comparisons of the authors' own data variants.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' classification is rejected. The study's scaling-law mention is background, and all results are the performance of its own method. Table 1 has no uncertainty estimates and Figures 3 and 4 have no numeric values. There is also an internal inconsistency about which model size (1.5B vs 7B) the unfiltered non-72B curve in Figure 4a uses.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss-law fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study uses synthetic text for continued pretraining, but does not test whether the same loss power law holds across modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream math and STEM accuracy against training-token scale and at some model sizes; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or fit a general downstream scaling law.

No scaling-law exponent or compute-optimal split fitting choices are compared. Some downstream accuracy curves plateau or degrade with data quality, but the study does not test the stated loss-law or allocation disagreements.

relation.reason: The introduction relies on scaling laws to motivate synthetic-data expansion; the reported results concern the authors' synthesis method and its ablations.

tranche.reason: Scaling laws motivate increasing training data; the experiments evaluate CCS performance and data-synthesis efficiency. They do not test power-law loss, extrapolation, compute allocation, architecture invariance, downstream prediction, or fitted-law dependence.

source_check.notes: The rows describe method comparisons and ablations, not independent tests of a claim version. Section 4.4 mentions a 7B unfiltered-data curve, although Appendix A.4 specifies 1.5B by default and Figure 4a explicitly labels only the 72B exceptions.
